citizen.blurb: The bite-sized pieces of language an AI actually works with.
citizen.standfirst: Why AI systems measure text in tokens instead of words, and what that quietly controls: chat limits, API pricing, and how far your prompt actually reaches.
citizen.core:
An arcade does not take cash at every machine. You trade cash for tokens first, then use those tokens to play. AI models work in a similar way. Before a model reads your text, a tokenizer turns it into tokens. The model then reads and writes one token at a time.

A token is not the same as a word. Short words such as "cat" may be one token. Longer words may split into several parts. Spaces, marks, and numbers can also use tokens. Token count depends on the language, type of text, and model. So word count is only a rough guide. The tokenizer gives the real count.
citizen.everyday:
A chatbot may reject a long message even when the word count looks fine. That is because its limit is measured in tokens, not words. The same token budget covers both your prompt and the assistant's reply.

Code, numbers, and rare words may use more tokens than plain text. If a request is too long, split it into smaller parts. Token limits can also affect how much of an old chat the model can keep in view.
citizen.businesses:
AI services often charge for input and output tokens at different rates. A support bot may send a large block of background text with every request, even when its reply is short. That hidden text can raise costs.

Token limits also shape what a product can handle. Long contracts, reports, and call transcripts must fit inside the model's context window. Different models may have different limits and token counts. Tracking tokens per request makes costs easier to plan.
citizen.appBuilders:
Use the tokenizer made for the target model. Models can use different tokenizers, so word counts and rough estimates may be wrong.

Token count affects whether a prompt fits, what it costs, and how you split long text. Leave some room below the model's limit instead of filling it fully.
citizen.modelBuilders:
The tokenizer is set before model training starts. Many models use a method called byte-pair encoding. Once training begins, changing the tokenizer usually means training the model again.

Vocabulary size is a trade-off. A larger vocabulary can make text use fewer tokens, but it also makes parts of the model larger. A tokenizer trained mostly on English may split other languages into more pieces. So the same idea can use more tokens in one language than another.
citizen.smalltalk: Tokens are like arcade coins for AI. A tokenizer turns your text into them, and the model reads them one at a time. That is why a long message can hit a token limit before it looks like a word limit.

technical.blurb: An integer index into a model's fixed subword vocabulary, produced by byte-pair encoding or a similar algorithm and converted to an embedding vector before any layer runs.
technical.standfirst: How byte-pair encoding and SentencePiece build a fixed vocabulary, why tokenizer choice varies by model family and can't change after pretraining, and the sequence-length-versus-embedding-cost trade-off in vocabulary size.
technical.core:
A token is an integer index into a model's fixed vocabulary. That vocabulary is built before pretraining starts, by a subword tokenization algorithm such as byte-pair encoding or a SentencePiece unigram model, run over a large text corpus. The algorithm merges character sequences that occur together often into single vocabulary entries. Common words often collapse into one token, while rarer words split into two or more subword pieces. Text is converted into a sequence of these IDs. Each ID is looked up in an embedding table, and the model's forward pass, through attention and feedforward layers, then operates on that sequence of vectors, several layers removed from the original characters.

A common engineering mistake is treating tokens-per-word as a fixed constant, often quoted as a rule of thumb like 0.75 words per token. That ratio holds loosely for English prose and nothing else — it shifts with script, morphology, and content type, so capacity planning built on a single conversion factor drifts as soon as input mixes in code, dense numerals, or a non-English language. The only dependable count comes from running the actual tokenizer for the target model, since a factor tuned to English misses other content.
technical.appBuilders:
Token counting has to happen with the tokenizer library for the specific model in use before a request is sent. That count determines whether a prompt fits inside the context window, what the call will cost, and how a document needs to be chunked for retrieval-augmented generation. Rate limits are frequently expressed in tokens per minute, so a handful of long-context calls can exhaust a quota that a much larger number of short calls would not touch. Portability across providers is limited by tokenizer differences as much as by API shape: the same prompt can consume noticeably more or fewer tokens on one model family than another, which changes both cost and whether it fits at all, sometimes forcing an entire re-chunking pass just to move a pipeline between vendors.

Streaming responses are delivered token-by-token. Perceived latency in a chat interface tracks generated token count directly. Truncation strategies for long inputs need to be built against the real count that tokenizer produces, since an assumed conversion factor drifts across document types.
technical.businesses:
Token-based pricing bills the two halves of a request — sent and returned — at different, independently changing rates. A deployment's real unit economics depend on typical input token volume (system prompt, retrieved context, history) as much as on output length, so cost modeling has to track full request composition alongside reply length. Generation latency and throughput scale with output token count too, which makes token volume a capacity-planning input as well as a billing line item.

Tokenizer differences between vendors add a migration cost that's easy to underweight: moving to a different model family can change both price and whether the same documents fit inside a context window, independent of the underlying task. Token-level request logs are also a practical basis for usage auditing in a regulated deployment, since they capture consumption at finer granularity than request counts alone, down to which stage of a pipeline actually drove the spend.
technical.modelBuilders:
Vocabulary size trades off against sequence length. A bigger vocabulary means shorter token sequences per document, which cuts compute. But it also grows the embedding table and the final softmax layer, since both scale with vocabulary size regardless of sequence length. Corpus makeup also affects fairness across languages. A vocabulary trained mostly on English splits other languages into more, shorter tokens, which raises their inference cost regardless of model size.

The tokenizer is frozen at the start of pretraining. Changing vocabulary later means retraining, or costly embedding surgery. Multilingual or domain-specific teams design the tokenizer early, before pretraining locks it in.
technical.smalltalk: A token is just an ID number for a chunk of text pulled from a fixed vocabulary the model was trained on — the model never actually sees words, only that stream of IDs, one prediction at a time.
